hmmt-nov-2022-guts-02.title: Glue letters together
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-02.body:
Gluing AB, CD, EF into single symbols leaves $26-3=23$ symbols, so there are $23!$ permutations with all three pairs contiguous: $p_1=\frac{23!}{26!}$. Gluing ABC and DEF leaves $26-4=22$ symbols, so $p_2=\frac{22!}{26!}$. Hence $\frac{p_1}{p_2}=\frac{23!}{22!}=23$.

**Answer: 23**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-03.title: Projection argument
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-03.body:
The circle has radius $\sqrt{2022}$, so the polygon must project onto the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis in intervals of length at least $2\sqrt{2022}$. A closed polygon with axis-parallel sides has horizontal edges covering the $x$-extent at least twice (once going right, once coming back) and likewise vertically, so the perimeter is at least $2\cdot2\sqrt{2022}+2\cdot2\sqrt{2022}=8\sqrt{2022}$. This is attained by the square circumscribed about the circle, of side $2\sqrt{2022}$.

**Answer: $8\sqrt{2022}$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-04.title: Coordinates
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-04.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(2,0)$, $C=(2,2)$, $D=(0,2)$. Then $X=(1,\sqrt3)$, $Y=(2-\sqrt3,1)$, $Z=(1,2-\sqrt3)$, and $W=(-\sqrt3,1)$ (outside, on the side of $DA$).

$WXYZ$ has perpendicular diagonals: $XZ$ is vertical of length $\sqrt3-(2-\sqrt3)=2\sqrt3-2$, and $WY$ is horizontal of length $(2-\sqrt3)-(-\sqrt3)=2$. Its area is $\frac12\cdot2\cdot(2\sqrt3-2)=2\sqrt3-2=-2+\sqrt{12}$, so $a=-2$, $b=12$ and $a+b=10$.

**Answer: 10**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-05.title: Eliminate with $C=xy$
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-05.body:
Rewrite as $xy+1=3y$ and $xy+2=3x$. With $C=xy$ we get $y=\frac{C+1}3$ and $x=\frac{C+2}3$, so $\frac{(C+1)(C+2)}9=C$, i.e. $C^2-6C+2=0$ and $C=3\pm\sqrt7$. Both roots give positive $x,y$, so the maximum is $3+\sqrt7$.

**Answer: $3+\sqrt7$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-06.title: Case on the center
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-06.body:
By the symmetry between the colors, let $O$ be blue and multiply the count by $2$. The equilateral triangles are: $OXY$ for adjacent hexagon vertices $X,Y$; the two large triangles $ACE$ and $BDF$.

Since $O$ is blue, no two adjacent hexagon vertices can both be blue. Each of $ACE$ and $BDF$ must contain a blue vertex (else it is all red), and neither may be entirely blue. A set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices has at most $3$ elements, and with $3$ it is $ACE$ or $BDF$, which is forbidden. So exactly two vertices are blue, non-adjacent, one in $\{A,C,E\}$ and one in $\{B,D,F\}$, i.e. they are opposite vertices: $3$ choices.

So there are $3$ good colorings with $O$ blue and $3$ with $O$ red, $6$ in total.

**Answer: 6**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-07.title: Count by length
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-07.body:
A $d$-digit binary number starts with $1$; it qualifies if the remaining $d-1$ digits contain $j$ ones with $1+j\ge d-1-j$. The counts for $d=1,\dots,9$ are $1,2,3,7,11,26,42,99,163$. The cumulative totals are $1,3,6,13,24,50,92,191,354$. Since $191<200\le354$, the $200$th number has $9$ digits (it is $301$, i.e. $100101101_2$).

**Answer: 9**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-08.title: Hamiltonian cycles
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-08.body:
We count Hamiltonian cycles of the $4\times4$ grid graph, each counted twice (two directions) once the starting square is fixed. Each corner square has only two neighbours, so every corner is a turn of the cycle (an L-shape), which restricts the shapes. Only two shapes of cycles survive: a "U" shape (the four orientations) and an "H"-type shape (the two orientations). That gives $4+2=6$ undirected cycles, so $2\cdot6=12$ paths.

**Answer: 12**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-09.title: Complete a parallelogram
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-09.body:
Let $E$ be the point on $CD$ with $ABED$ a parallelogram, so $DE=AB$, $BE=AD$ and $BE\parallel AD$. Then $EC=CD-DE=CD-AB=AD=EB$, so triangle $EBC$ is isosceles with $EB=EC$. Since $AB\parallel CD$, $\angle BCE=\angle BCD=180^\circ-\angle ABC=55^\circ$, so $\angle BEC=180^\circ-2\cdot55^\circ=70^\circ$. As $BE\parallel AD$, $\angle ADC=\angle BEC=70^\circ$.

**Answer: $70^\circ$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-10.title: Reduce to one period
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-10.body:
Let $y=\frac x{2.5}$, uniform on $[0,400]$; we need $\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor y\rfloor}{2.5}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac y{2.5}\right\rfloor$. Write $y=5a+b$ with $a$ an integer and $0\le b<5$. Then $\left\lfloor\frac{5a+\lfloor b\rfloor}{2.5}\right\rfloor=2a+\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor b\rfloor}{2.5}\right\rfloor$ and $\left\lfloor\frac{5a+b}{2.5}\right\rfloor=2a+\left\lfloor\frac b{2.5}\right\rfloor$. So we need $\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor b\rfloor}{2.5}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac b{2.5}\right\rfloor$ for $b\in[0,5)$, which fails exactly for $b\in[2.5,3)$ (there $\lfloor b\rfloor=2$ gives $0$ but $\frac b{2.5}\ge1$). The probability is $1-\frac{0.5}{5}=\frac9{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac9{10}$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-11.title: Right triangle altitude
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-11.body:
Here $AB=11+27=38$ and $CD=34$. Drop perpendiculars from $A,P,B$ to line $CD$ with feet $A',P',B'$. Since $A'B'=AB=38$ and $CD=34$, and the trapezoid is isosceles, $A'D=CB'=2$ (the feet lie $2$ units beyond $D$ and $C$). Then $A'P'=AP=11$ gives $P'D=11-2=9$ and $P'C=34-9=25$. In the right triangle $CPD$ (right angle at $P$) the altitude from $P$ satisfies $PP'^2=P'D\cdot P'C=9\cdot25$, so the height of the trapezoid is $PP'=15$.

**Answer: 15**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-12.title: Distance as a sum of speeds
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-12.body:
Suppose she starts at $n$ mph and drives for $t$ minutes, so her speeds are $n,n-1,\dots,m+1$ (with $m=n-t$) each for one minute, $m\ge0$. The distance in miles is
$$\frac1{60}\sum_{j=m+1}^{n}j=\frac{n(n+1)-m(m+1)}{120}=\frac{(n+m+1)(n-m)}{120}=\frac23,$$
so $(n+m+1)(n-m)=80$. Here $n+m+1>n-m$ and the two factors have opposite parity, so $(n+m+1,\,n-m)\in\{(80,1),(16,5)\}$. The case $n-m=1$ means she drives only one minute at constant speed, not slower on arrival, which is excluded. So $n-m=5$ (with $n=10$, $m=5$: speeds $10,9,8,7,6$, distance $\frac{40}{60}=\frac23$), and she drives for $5$ minutes: she gets home at $5{:}05$ PM.

**Answer: 5:05 PM**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-13.title: Pair each path with its complement
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-13.body:
For each path, the region below the path (between it and the $x$-axis, up to $x=6$) together with the region above the path (inside the $6\times3$ rectangle) fills the rectangle of area $18$. Reflecting a path through the center of the rectangle swaps the two regions, so the sum of the areas under all paths equals half of $18$ times the number of paths: $\frac{18}2\binom93=9\cdot84=756$.

**Answer: 756**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-14.title: Exponentiate
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-14.body:
Let $a=10^x$, $b=10^y$. The equations become $10a=\frac b{10}+1$ and $10b=a+1$. Subtracting, $10a-10b=\frac b{10}-a$, so $11a=\frac{101}{10}b$, hence $\frac ab=10^{x-y}=\frac{101}{110}$. (The linear system has a positive solution, so such $x,y$ exist.)

**Answer: $\frac{101}{110}$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-15.title: Vertex values
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-15.body:
A quadratic with $a>0$ is minimized at the average of its roots. For $a(x-b)(x-c)$ the minimum is $k=-\frac{a(b-c)^2}4$; for $a(x-b)(x+c)$ it is $l=-\frac{a(b+c)^2}4$. So
$$k-l=\frac a4\left[(b+c)^2-(b-c)^2\right]=abc.$$
The maximum product of three distinct elements is $9\cdot10\cdot11=990$.

**Answer: 990**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-16.title: Factor the polynomial
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-16.body:
Note that $\sin\theta\,x^2+(\cos\theta+\tan\theta)x+1=(\tan\theta\,x+1)(\cos\theta\,x+1)$, because $\tan\theta\cos\theta=\sin\theta$.

- If $\sin\theta=0$, then $\tan\theta=0$ and $\cos\theta=\pm1$, so $P(x)=\pm x+1$ is linear with exactly one root. So $\sin\theta=0$ works.
- If $\sin\theta\ne0$, $P$ is a quadratic with roots $-\cot\theta$ and $-\sec\theta$; it has only one real root iff they coincide: $\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\frac1{\cos\theta}$, i.e. $\cos^2\theta=\sin\theta$, i.e. $\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta-1=0$. Then $\sin\theta=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt5}2$, and only $\frac{\sqrt5-1}2$ lies in $[-1,1]$.

So the possible values are $\sin\theta=0$ and $\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt5-1}2$.

**Answer: $0$ and $\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-17.title: Colorings mod 7
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-17.body:
The coloring has period $7$, so it suffices to color the residues $0,\dots,6$ and compute mod $7$. The forbidden pattern is: $k,k+1,2k$ all the same colour. Take $0$ red (multiply by $2$ at the end).

- $k=0$: $(0,1,0)$, so $1$ is blue.
- $k=1$: $(1,2,2)$, so $2$ is red.
- Case $3$ red: $k=2$ gives $(2,3,4)$, so $4$ is blue; $k=4$ gives $(4,5,1)$ so $5$ is red; $k=6$ gives $(6,0,5)$ so $6$ is blue. This is the coloring RBRRBRB (colors of $0,\dots,6$). It is consistent.
- Case $3$ blue: if $4$ were blue, $(4,5,1)$ forces $5$ red and $(3,4,6)$ forces $6$ red, and then $(6,0,5)$ is all red, a contradiction. So $4$ is red. Now $5$ and $6$ cannot both be red ($(6,0,5)$) nor both blue ($(5,6,3)$), giving the two colorings RBRBRRB and RBRBRBR.

So there are $3$ colorings with $0$ red, and $6$ in total.

**Answer: 6**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-18.title: Shadow is a square with diagonals = opposite edges
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-18.body:
Imagine the shadow of the skeleton of the tetrahedron. The diagonals of the square shadow must be the shadows of a pair of opposite edges. Both of these edges must be parallel to the plane: otherwise the four edges forming the sides of the square would not all be equal in length. Hence each diagonal of the square has length equal to the edge length of the tetrahedron. A square of area $16$ has diagonal $4\sqrt2$, so the edge length is $4\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $4\sqrt2$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-19.title: Descents of the inverse
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-19.body:
For a permutation $p$, let $f_k(p)$ be the least number of copies needed to get $1,\dots,k$ as a subsequence. If $k$ appears before $k+1$ in $p$ then $f_{k+1}=f_k$; otherwise $f_{k+1}=f_k+1$. Since $f_1=1$, the annoyingness is $1+\#\{k:\ k+1\text{ appears before }k\}$. Each of the $2021$ values of $k$ has this property with probability $\frac12$, so by linearity of expectation the answer is $1+\frac{2021}2=\frac{2023}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{2023}{2}$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-20.title: Angle bisector in the cyclic quadrilateral
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-20.body:
Because $BACT$ is cyclic, $\angle BTA=\angle BCA=45^\circ=\angle CBA=\angle CTA$, so $TA$ bisects $\angle BTC$, and $\angle BTC=90^\circ$ (it subtends diameter $BC$). By the angle bisector theorem in $\triangle TBC$ (with $A$-ray meeting $BC$ at $N$): $\frac{BT}{TC}=\frac{BN}{NC}=\frac13$. Then $TC=3BT$ and $BT^2+TC^2=BC^2=AB^2+AC^2=200$, so $10BT^2=200$, $BT^2=20$. The area is $\frac12BT\cdot TC=\frac32BT^2=30$.

**Answer: 30**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-22.title: Pair up $(a,b)$ with $(57-b,57-a)$
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-22.body:
No pair with $b=57$ works (as $b^2\equiv0$), so consider $1\le a<b\le56$. The map $(a,b)\mapsto(57-b,57-a)$ is an involution on these pairs, and $(57-b)^2\equiv b^2$, $(57-a)^2\equiv a^2\pmod{57}$, so it swaps the two remainders. If $a^2\not\equiv b^2$, exactly one pair of $\{(a,b),(57-b,57-a)\}$ satisfies "$a^2\bmod57<b^2\bmod57$" (a fixed pair would need $a=57-b$, which forces $a^2\equiv b^2$). So the answer is $\frac12\left[\binom{56}2-X\right]$, where $X$ counts pairs $a<b\le56$ with $a^2\equiv b^2\pmod{57}$.

To find $X$ count ordered pairs $(a,b)$ in $1..57$ with $(a-b)(a+b)\equiv0$ modulo both $3$ and $19$. There are $2\cdot3-1=5$ residue pairs modulo $3$ and $2\cdot19-1=37$ modulo $19$, so $185$ ordered pairs by CRT, including the $57$ with $a=b$. Only $a=b=57$ involves $57$. So there are $185-57=128$ ordered pairs with $a\ne b$, within $1..56$, and $X=64$.

The answer is $\frac12(1540-64)=738$.

**Answer: 738**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-23.title: The minimum is at $C$
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-23.body:
Take $P=C$. For any other point $O$, moving from $O$ to $C$ changes the quantity $AP+2BP+3CP$ by
$$(AC-AO)+2(BC-BO)+3(0-CO)\le OC+2\,OC-3\,OC=0,$$
using $AC\le AO+OC$ and $BC\le BO+OC$. So the value at $C$ is at most the value at any other point, and the minimum is $AC+2BC+3\cdot0=2022+2\cdot2023=6068$. (Physically: the pull of strength $3$ toward $C$ outweighs the pulls $1+2$ toward $A$ and $B$.)

**Answer: 6068**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-24.title: Append a letter and remove bad endings
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-24.body:
A string of length $n$ is untranslatable only if its first $n-1$ letters form an untranslatable string. Appending any of the $4$ letters to an untranslatable string of length $n-1$ gives $4a_{n-1}$ strings, and the ones that are not untranslatable are exactly those that end in AUG, whose first $n-3$ letters form an untranslatable string (AUG cannot overlap itself), giving $a_{n-3}$ of them. So $a_n=4a_{n-1}-a_{n-3}$ for $n\ge3$, and $(x,y,z)=(4,0,-1)$.

**Answer: $(4,0,-1)$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-25.title: Rotation about $P$
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-25.body:
$ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid with $P$ as its circumcenter ($PA=PD=PB=PC$). Construct the isosceles trapezoid $AB'BC$ (so $BB'\parallel AC$). Then $AB'PD$ is a rhombus, so $\angle B'CD=\frac12\angle B'PD=60^\circ$ by the inscribed angle theorem. Also $B'C=11$ because quadrilateral $B'APC$ is a $60^\circ$ rotation of $ADPB$ about $P$. In triangle $B'CD$ with $B'C=11$, $CD=13$ and $\angle C=60^\circ$, the law of cosines gives $B'D^2=121+169-143=147$, so $B'D=7\sqrt3$. As $AB'PD$ is a rhombus with $\angle B'PD=120^\circ$, $B'D=AP\sqrt3$, so $AP=7$.

**Answer: 7**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-26.title: Fix the last digit
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-26.body:
Count by the last digit, then the first digit. For a number with $L$ digits, the middle digits can be chosen in the same number of ways whatever the first and last digits are, so we can compare the weights of the (first, last) digit pairs: the first digit is nonzero. For last digit $0$ there are $9$ choices for the first digit; for any nonzero last digit there are $8$ choices for the first digit (nonzero and different from the last).

Even last digits: $0,2,4,6,8$ with weights $9+4\cdot8=41$. All last digits: $9+9\cdot8=81$. So the probability is $\frac{41}{81}$.

**Answer: $\frac{41}{81}$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-27.title: Classify the pieces
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-27.body:
Each piece has area $\frac18$ and all interior angles $45^\circ$ or $90^\circ$, so it can only be a triangle or a quadrilateral. The possible shapes are:

- right isosceles triangles with legs $\frac12$;
- $1\times\frac18$ rectangles;
- $\frac12\times\frac14$ rectangles.

*Triangles:* the square is split into four quadrants, each cut by one of its two diagonals: $2^4=16$ ways.

*$1\times\frac18$ rectangles:* all horizontal or all vertical: $2$ ways.

*$\frac12\times\frac14$ rectangles* (the delicate case). Label the quadrants $A,B$ (top) and $C,D$ (bottom). If every rectangle lies inside one quadrant, each quadrant is cut into two rectangles in $2$ ways, so $2^4=16$ ways. If rectangles span the top pair of quadrants but not the others: $4$ ways; similarly $4$ ways for each of the other three adjacent pairs (that is $16$ ways). If rectangles span both the top pair and the bottom pair: $1$ way; both the left pair and the right pair: $1$ way. There are $2$ more configurations. In total this case gives $16+4+4+4+4+1+1+2=36$ ways.

The total is $16+2+36=54$.

**Answer: 54**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-28.title: Midpoint of the two apexes
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-28.body:
Let $T$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$ to $BC$ ($BT=5$, $CT=9$, altitude $12$). Triangles $PQR\sim ABC$ with $P\leftrightarrow A$ have two positions $P_1,P_2$ (mirror images over $QR$), and their altitude foot $T'$ on $QR$ is their common midpoint's projection, so the sum of the distances from $P_1,P_2$ to $BC$ is $2\,d(T',BC)$. Since $T'$ divides $QR$ in the ratio $QT':T'R=BT:TC=5:9$,
$$d(T',BC)=\frac{9\,d(Q,BC)+5\,d(R,BC)}{14}.$$
By similar triangles, $QB\perp BC$ with $QB=\frac{12\cdot14}{9}$ and $RC=\frac{12\cdot14}{5}$ (so $d(Q,BC)=\frac{168}9$ and $d(R,BC)=\frac{168}5$), which gives $d(T',BC)=\frac{168+168}{14}=24$. The required sum is $2\cdot24=48$. (Numerically: $P_1=(-7.8,36)$, $P_2=(17.8,12)$ with $B=(0,0)$, $C=(14,0)$, $A=(5,12)$, so $36+12=48$.)

**Answer: 48**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-29.title: Reduce to a quadratic inequality
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-29.body:
Write $z=a+bi$. Then $|z^2+2|^2=(a^2-b^2+2)^2+(2ab)^2=(a^2+b^2)^2+4(a^2-b^2)+4$. So $z\in S$ iff $x^2+4(a^2-b^2)+4\le x$ where $x=a^2+b^2$. Let $a^2-b^2=cx$ with $|c|<1$: the condition is $x^2+(4c-1)x+4\le0$. This has a real solution $x>0$ iff the discriminant $(4c-1)^2-16\ge0$ and the roots are positive, i.e. $4c-1\le-4$, so $c\le-\frac34$ (and $c\ge-1$). The ratio $\frac{b^2}{a^2}=\frac{1-c}{1+c}$ is smallest for the largest $c$, i.e. $c=-\frac34$, giving $a^2:b^2=1:7$ and $\tan\theta=\frac ba\ge\sqrt7$. Equality occurs at $x=2$, i.e. $z=\frac12+\frac{\sqrt7}2i$.

**Answer: $\sqrt7$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-30.title: Reflect $A$ across the perpendicular bisector
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-30.body:
Redefine $D$ as the reflection of $A$ across the perpendicular bisector $\ell$ of $BC$. We show that $DB$ and $DC$ are tangent to $\omega$, so this is the same point as in the problem. Since $\angle CBM=\angle CAM=\angle BAM=\angle BCM$, we have $MB=MC$, so $M$ lies on $\ell$ and $\omega$ is symmetric about $\ell$. Reflecting the tangent lines $AB$, $AC$ across $\ell$ gives tangents $DC$, $DB$ to $\omega$.

The reflection $D$ lies on the circumcircle (its center is on $\ell$), and $ADCB$ is an isosceles trapezoid with $AD\parallel BC$, $DC=AB=8$, $BD=AC=12$. Ptolemy's theorem on this cyclic quadrilateral (diagonals $AC$ and $BD$) gives $AC\cdot BD=AD\cdot BC+AB\cdot DC$, i.e. $144=5\,AD+64$. So $AD=16$.

**Answer: 16**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-31.title: Sort and compare consecutive terms
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-31.body:
Assume $a_1\le a_2\le\cdots\le a_{2023}$. Then
$$a_{k+1}-a_k=\sum_i\left(|a_{k+1}-a_i|-|a_k-a_i|\right)=k(a_{k+1}-a_k)-(2023-k)(a_{k+1}-a_k)=(2k-2023)(a_{k+1}-a_k).$$
So $a_{k+1}=a_k$ unless $2k-2023=1$, i.e. $k=1012$. Hence $a_1=\cdots=a_{1012}=p$ and $a_{1013}=\cdots=a_{2023}=q$ with $q>p$, and the condition for $a_1$: $p=1011(q-p)$, so $1012p=1011q$, i.e. $(p,q)=(1011c,1012c)$ for a positive integer $c$ (the condition for $a_{2023}$ gives the same relation). The smallest sum is for $c=1$: $1012\cdot1011+1011\cdot1012=2046264$.

**Answer: 2046264**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-32.title: The $120^\circ$ lemma
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-32.body:
*Lemma.* If $\angle X=120^\circ$ in $\triangle XYZ$ and the bisector from $X$ meets $YZ$ at $T$, then $\frac1{XY}+\frac1{XZ}=\frac1{XT}$. (Take $W$ on $XY$ with $XWT$ equilateral; then $TW\parallel XZ$ and $\frac{XT}{XZ}=\frac{YT}{YX}=1-\frac{XT}{XY}$.)

The three angles at $P$ are $120^\circ$ each, and $PD$ bisects $\angle BPC$, etc. The lemma gives $\frac1{PB}+\frac1{PC}=\frac1{PD}=4$, $\frac1{PC}+\frac1{PA}=\frac1{PE}=5$, $\frac1{PA}+\frac1{PB}=\frac1{PF}=7$. Adding and halving, $\frac1{PA}+\frac1{PB}+\frac1{PC}=8$, so $\frac1{PA}=4$, $\frac1{PB}=3$, $\frac1{PC}=1$. Therefore $AP+BP+CP=\frac14+\frac13+1=\frac{19}{12}$.

**Answer: $\frac{19}{12}$**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-33.title: Indicators and modular arithmetic
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-33.body:
Let $n=2k+1=101$ (so $k=50$ here) and let $I_i$ indicate that Dalmathian $i$ voted for the winner. Then $E[X^2]=nE[I_1]+n(n-1)E[I_1I_2]$.

$E[I_1]=\frac12+\frac{\binom{2k}k}{2^{2k+1}}$ (given his vote, at least $k$ of the other $2k$ must agree: exactly $k$, or half of the rest by symmetry). $E[I_1I_2]=\frac12\left(\frac12+\frac{\binom{2k-1}{k-1}}{2^{2k-1}}\right)$. Simplifying,
$$E[X^2]=\frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{2^{2k+1}}(2k+1)^2+\frac{(2k+1)(2k+2)}4.$$
For $k=50$ the fraction $\frac ab$ is this value, and $k$ with $103\mid a-bk$ is the value of $\frac ab$ in the field $\mathbb F_{103}$. Using Wilson's theorem ($102!\equiv-1$), Fermat's little theorem ($2^{102}\equiv1$, so $2^{-101}\equiv2$) and $4^{-1}\equiv26$, the value is $51$ (also confirmed by evaluating $E[X^2]$ exactly).

**Answer: 51**

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-34.title: Estimation
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-34.body:
Official answer: $L\approx23.120$ (from $10^7$ simulations; standard deviation about $10^{-3}$). An estimate $E$ earns $\left\lfloor20\min(E/L,L/E)^{10}\right\rfloor$ points.

Heuristic: the probability that a given center has a palindrome of length $2n+1$ is about $2^{-n}$, so among about $1000$ centers one expects palindromes of length $2n+1$ when $2^{-n}\cdot1000\gtrsim1$, i.e. $n\approx10$, so lengths around $21$ are common and sometimes longer ones occur. This suggests a guess a bit above $21$.

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-35.title: Estimation
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-35.body:
Official answer: $P\approx0.003679$ (from $10^9$ simulations). An estimate $E$ earns $\left\lfloor20\min(E/P,P/E)\right\rfloor$ points.

Heuristic: the individual probabilities $P(a_{i+1}>a_i)$ are $\frac78,\frac79,\frac{23}{32},\frac{17}{25},\frac{47}{72},\frac{31}{49},\frac{79}{128},\frac{49}{81},\frac{119}{200}$. Their product is about $0.05$. The events are positively dependent in the wrong direction: conditioned on $a_1<\cdots<a_k$, the value $a_k$ tends to be large, making $a_k<a_{k+1}$ less likely, which reduces the answer by roughly a factor $10$ over nine inequalities.

hmmt-nov-2022-guts-36.title: Estimation
hmmt-nov-2022-guts-36.body: Official answer: $M=8+8\sqrt[4]3\approx18.5285921$. An estimate $E$ earns $\left\lfloor20\min(E/M,M/E)^4\right\rfloor$ points. The intended method is to look at the answers of earlier problems in the round (or the other rounds) to get a rough estimate of the median.
